because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness through the man whom he appointed. He has given assurance of this to all by raising him from the dead."
When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, but others said: "We will hear you about this again."
And so Paul went out from among them.
But some followed him and believed. Among them were Dionysius the Areopagite, his wife, named Damaris, and others with them.
After this Paul left the Athenians and came to Corinth.

There he found a certain Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had just come from Italy, and Priscilla his wife, because Claudius Caesar had ordered all Jews to be expelled from Rome. He went to them,
and because they practiced the same craft, he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.
Every Sabbath he spoke in the synagogue and tried to persuade Jews and Gentiles.
When Silas and Timothy came from Macedonia, the Spirit pressed Paul, and he testified to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.
But when they opposed him and blasphemed, he shook out his garment at them and said to them: "Your blood be on your own heads! May I be innocent! From now on I will go to the Gentiles."
He left there and went into the house of a man named Titius, son of Justus, a worshipper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue.
Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord together with his whole household. Many Corinthians listened to him, believed and were baptized.
The Lord said to Paul at night in a vision: "Do not be afraid, but speak and do not be silent,
for I am with you, and no one will lay a hand on you to do you harm, for I have many people in this city."
And he stayed there one year and six months, and taught the word of God among them.
But when Gallio was governor of Achaia, all the Jews rose up together against Paul and brought him before the judgment seat,
and they said: "This man is going against the law and stirring people up to worship God."
And as Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews: "If it were a crime of some kind, one of the offenses, O Jews, I would have heard you out as your words require;
but if it is some dispute about words and names and your law, see to it yourselves, for I do not wish to be a judge of such things."
And he drove them away from the judgment seat.
Then all the Gentiles seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the judgment seat; and Gallio did not care about any of it.
But Paul stayed there many days, and then took leave of the brethren and sailed away to Syria, and Priscilla and Aquila went with him. He had his hair cut at Cenchreae, for he had taken a vow.
He arrived at Ephesus and left them there, and he himself went into the synagogue and spoke to the Jews.
When they begged him to stay there, he did not wish to,
but took leave of them and said: "I will come back again, if God wills." He boarded a ship from Ephesus
and went down to Caesarea; he went up and greeted the church, and went on to Antioch.
And he spent some time there and departed, and went from place to place, one after another, through the regions of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
There was a certain Jew named Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth, an eloquent man, who came to Ephesus; he was powerful in the Scriptures.
He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit he spoke and taught accurately about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John.
And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue. Aquila and Priscilla heard him, and they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.
And as he wished to cross over to Achaia, the brethren wrote to the disciples there telling them to welcome him. When he arrived, he helped those who had believed through grace,
for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.
While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul passed through the upper regions and came to Ephesus, and there he found some disciples.
And he said to them: "Have you received the Holy Spirit, and do you believe?" But they said to him: "We have not even heard of the Holy Spirit."
Paul said to them: "Then into what were you baptized?" And they said: "Into John's baptism."
Paul said to them: "John baptized the people with a baptism of repentance, and told them to believe in the one who would come after him, that is, Jesus Christ."
And when they heard this, they were baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.
And when Paul laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.
There were twelve of those men in all.
And he went into the synagogue and spoke boldly there for three months, speaking with them and persuading them about the kingdom of God.

But when some of them grew angry and became disobedient, and spoke evil of the Way before the crowd, he withdrew from them, took the disciples away with him, and spoke every day in the school of Tyrannus.
And this went on for two years, until all who lived in Asia, both Jews and Gentiles, had heard the word of the Lord.
God worked no small miracles by the hands of Paul,
so that people even took handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched his sweat and brought them to the sick, and their diseases left them and the unclean spirits went out.
Some of the travelling Jewish exorcists began to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying: "We adjure you by Jesus, whom Paul preaches."
Those who did this were the seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish chief priest.
The evil spirit answered them: "Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?"
And the man who had the unclean spirit sprang up, overpowered both of them and attacked them, until they fled from that house naked and wounded.
This became known to all the Jews and Gentiles who lived in Ephesus. Fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
And many of the believers came and confessed their deeds.
And many who had practised evil arts gathered their books and burned them in front of everyone. They counted up their value and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver.
So the word of the Lord grew strongly and spread.
When these things were finished, Paul resolved in his heart to go to Jerusalem after passing through Macedonia and Achaia, and he said: "After I have been there, I must also see Rome."
And he sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself stayed for a time in Asia.
At that time there was no small fear concerning the Way.
For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, made silver shrines of Artemis and brought the craftsmen no small amount of work.
He gathered those who made such things and said: "Men, you know that our livelihood comes from this work.
And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but throughout almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods.

This is not only a hardship for us, that this position of ours is in danger of being discredited; the temple of the great goddess Artemis is also in danger of being held in contempt, and her wealth destroyed, she whom all Asia and the world worship."
When they heard this, they were filled with rage and cried out, saying: "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
The whole city was filled with confusion. They rushed together into the theatre and seized Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's companions, from the company.
Paul wanted to go in among the people, but the disciples would not let him.
Some of the rulers of Asia, who were his friends, sent to him and told him not to give himself up to the theatre.
Some were shouting one thing and some another, because the crowd was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had gathered.
From the crowd they brought forward Alexander, because the Jews put him forward. Alexander waved his hand to the crowd and wanted to make a defence to the people.
When they realized that he was a Jew, they all shouted together with one voice for about two hours, crying out and saying, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"

The town clerk of the people waved his hand and said to them, "Men of the people, Ephesians, who is there among men who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is the temple-keeper of the great Artemis and of the Diopetes?
Since this cannot be denied, you ought to be calm and do nothing rash.
You have brought these men here, who are neither robbers of temples nor blasphemers of our goddess.
If Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, let them bring the merchants of the market quarters. There are rulers; let them bring charges against one another.
If there is anything else to be looked into, let it be settled in a lawful assembly.

We are in danger of being accused of rioting because of today, since there was no reason for it, and we would not be able to give an account of this gathering." When he had said this, he dismissed the assembly.
After the uproar had died down, Paul called the disciples, comforted them, took his leave, and set out to go to Macedonia.
He went through those regions and comforted them with many words, and from there he went to Greece.
He was there for three months. There too the Jews plotted against him. As he was about to go up to Syria, he decided to return by way of Macedonia.
Accompanying him as far as Asia were Sosipater son of Pyrrhus, a Beroean; the Thessalonians Aristarchus and Secundus; Gaius of Derbe; Timothy; and the Asians Tychicus and Trophimus.
These went on ahead of us and waited for us at Troas.
We sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and came to them at Troas on the fifth day, and we stayed there seven days.
On the first day of the week we were gathered to bless the bread. Paul was speaking to them the word of teaching, because he was going to leave the next day, and he kept on speaking until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered.
A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window. While Paul spoke for a long time, he was overcome by deep sleep. Asleep, he fell from the third storey to the ground and lay dead.
Paul went down, threw himself on him, embraced him and said, "Do not be alarmed, because his life is still in him."
He went back up from there, blessed the bread and ate. He talked with them for a long time, until dawn, and then he left.
They brought the boy back alive and were greatly comforted.
We went on ahead by ship and went up to Assos, where we intended to take Paul aboard, because he had arranged it this way, planning to come on foot himself.
When he came to us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene.
From there we sailed the next day and arrived opposite Chios. In the evening we came to Samos, and on the following day to Miletus.
Paul wanted to sail past Ephesus, so that he would not spend a long time in Asia, for he was hurrying to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost, if that were possible for him.
And from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called for the elders of the church.
When they came to him, he said to them: "You yourselves know how I was with you the whole time, from the first day that I came into Asia,
and how I served the Lord with all humility, with tears and with trials, which happened to me because of the evil plots of the Jews;
how I held back nothing that was useful to you, but told it to you and taught you in public and in houses.
I testified to Jews and Gentiles about repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem bound in the spirit, and I do not know what will happen to me there,
except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in city after city and tells me that bonds and afflictions are waiting for me.

But I have not counted myself more precious than my soul, so that I may finish my course and my ministry, which I received from the Lord Jesus Christ: the testimony and the gospel of the grace of God.
And now, behold, I know that none of you, among whom I went about preaching the kingdom, will see my face again.
And so I testify to you on this very day that I am innocent of the blood of all of you,
for I held back nothing, but told you the whole counsel of God.
So take care of yourselves and of the whole flock, over which the Holy Spirit has appointed you as overseers and shepherds of the churches of God, which he acquired with his own blood.
I know that after I leave, savage wolves will come in among you, who will not spare the flock.
And men from among you will rise up and speak perverse things, to draw the disciples away to follow them.
Therefore stay awake, and remember that for three years, night and day, I did not stop teaching each one of you.
And now I entrust you to God, brothers, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you an inheritance among all the saints.
My heart did not covet anyone's silver, gold or clothing.
You yourselves know that these hands of mine provided for my needs and for those who were with me.
And I showed you in everything that by working hard in this way one must help the weak and remember the word of the Lord Jesus, for he said: 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'"
When he had said this, he knelt down with all of them and prayed.
Everyone wept loudly, and they embraced Paul and kissed him,
weeping most of all over the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they went with him to the ship.
And when we had boarded the ship and parted from them, we sailed quickly and reached Cos, the next day Rhodes, and from there Patara.
And we found a ship crossing over to Phoenicia; we went on board and set sail in it.
When Cyprus came into view, we left it on our left and sailed on to Syria and reached Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo.
And we sought out the brothers and stayed there just seven days. Through the Spirit they told Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
And when the seven days were over, we left and went on our way. They all saw us off, with their households and children, until we were outside the city. They knelt down on the seashore and prayed.
We said goodbye to one another and boarded the ship, and they went back to their own homes.
And we sailed on from Tyre and reached Ptolemais. We greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day.
The next day we left there and came to Caesarea. We went into the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
He had four daughters who were prophetesses.
And we stayed there many days. A prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul's belt, bound his feet and hands with it, and said: "The Holy Spirit says this: 'In this way the Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and hand him over to the gentiles.'"
When we heard this, we and the people of that place begged him not to go up to Jerusalem.

Then Paul answered us and said: "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem. I am prepared for the sake of the name of the Lord Jesus."
And since we could not persuade him, we fell silent and said: "May the will of God be done."
After those days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem.
Some disciples from Caesarea also came with us. We also brought along the man we stayed with, Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple.
When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us joyfully.
The next day Paul went with us to James, and all the elders came.
He greeted them and told them in detail, one thing after another, what God had done among the gentiles through his ministry.
When they heard this, they glorified God and said to him: "Brother, do you see how many tens of thousands of believers there are among the Jews? All of them are zealous for the law.

Some people say about you that you teach the Jews who live among the gentiles to turn away from Moses. Some people say about you that you tell them not to circumcise their children and not to live by the customs.
So what is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.
Do what I tell you. There are four men among us who have taken a vow on themselves.

Take these men, and purify yourself with them, so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that what people say about you is nothing, and that you yourself also live by the law and keep it.

As for the gentiles who have believed, we wrote and ordered that they need not observe anything of the kind, except that they keep away from what has been sacrificed to idols, from blood, and from fornication."

Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself with them. He went into the temple to give notice of when the days of purification would be completed, at which point the offering would be made for each one of them.
As the seven days were being completed, the Jews who were from Asia saw him in the temple. They stirred up all the people and laid their hands on him, and

they cried out: "Men of Israel, help me! This is the man who plots evil against the people, the law and this place, and teaches the same to everyone everywhere. And on top of that he has brought Gentiles into the temple and defiled this holy place."
For they had earlier seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred up, and there was a great uproar among the people. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the doors were shut.
And as they were about to kill him, word reached the tribune of the troops that all Jerusalem was gathered.
At once he took soldiers and centurions and came down on them. When they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Then the tribune came up, took him, and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He asked who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd shouted one thing and some another. Since he could not find out the truth because of the uproar, he ordered him to be taken to the barracks.
When he reached the steps, Paul had to be carried up by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,
for the mass of the people followed, crying out and saying: "Away with him!"
As he was being brought into the barracks, Paul said to the tribune: "May I say something to you?" He replied: "Do you know Greek?
Or are you the Egyptian who some time ago stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Sicarii out into the wilderness?"
Paul said to him: "I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people."
When he had given him permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned to the people with his hand. When there was silence, he spoke to them in the Hebrew language and said:
"Men, brothers and fathers, listen to the defense I now make to you."
When they heard that he was speaking to them in the Hebrew language, they became even quieter. And he said:

"I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia but brought up in this city. I was educated at the feet of Gamaliel and taught strictly according to the law of our fathers. I was zealous for God, just as all of you are today.
I persecuted this Way to the death, binding both men and women and handing them over to prison,
as the high priest and all the elders can testify about me. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I was going to Damascus to bring the people there back in chains to be punished.
As I was on my way and drawing near to Damascus, about midday, a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me.
I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me: 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?'
I answered: 'Who are you, Lord?' He said to me: 'I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.'
The people who were with me saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the one speaking to me.
I said: 'What shall I do, Lord?' And the Lord said to me: 'Get up and go into Damascus. There you will be told what you have been ordered to do.'
And since I could not see because of the glory of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and I entered Damascus.
There was a man named Ananias, a God-fearing man according to the law, who was well spoken of by all the Jews living in Damascus.
He came to me, stood over me and said to me: "Brother Saul, receive your sight." And at that very moment I received my sight and looked at him.
And he said: "The God of our fathers has chosen you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth,
for you shall be his witness to all people of what you have seen and heard.
And now, do not delay at all. Get up, be baptized, wash away your sins and call on his name."
And it happened, when I returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, that I fell into a trance
and saw the Lord, and he said to me: "Hurry and get out of Jerusalem quickly, for they will not accept your testimony about me."
And I said: "Lord, they themselves know that I was the one who handed over to prison and tormented in the synagogues those who believed in you.
And when the blood of your witness Stephen was being shed, I too was standing by and guarding the garments of those who killed him."
And he said to me: "Go, for I will send you to the nations far away."
They listened to him up to this word. Then they raised their voices and said: "Rid the earth of such a man, for he is not fit to live!"
And as they were shouting, they were throwing off their garments and flinging dust up into the air.
The tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks and said: "I will examine him under torture, so that I may learn for what crime they are shouting against him like this."
And as they were stretching him out with straps, Paul said to the centurion who was standing there: "Is it lawful for you to torture a Roman man who has not been tried?"
When the centurion heard this, he told the tribune and said: "What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman."
The tribune came to him and said to Paul: "Tell me, are you a Roman?" And he said: "Yes."
The tribune answered and said: "I obtained this privilege with a great sum of money." And Paul said: "But I was born in it."
Then those who were about to torture him immediately drew back from him, and the tribune was afraid when he realized that he was a Roman and that he had been entrusted to him.

On the next day, wishing to find out more truly why the Jews were accusing him like this, he released him and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to assemble. They brought Paul and set him in their midst.
Paul looked at the council and said: "Men, brothers, I have lived before God with a fully good conscience up to this very day."
But the high priest Ananias ordered those standing by to strike him on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him: "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall! You sit as a judge according to the law, and yet against the law you order me to be struck?"
And those standing by said to him: "Do you insult God's high priest?"
Paul said: "I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written: 'You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.'"

When Paul realized that one part of the council was Sadducees and the other part Pharisees, he cried out in the council: "Men, brothers, I am a Pharisee and the son of a Pharisee; I am being judged over the hope and the resurrection of the dead."
When he had said this, a great dissension arose between the Sadducees and the Pharisees, and the crowd of the people was [?] divided.
For the Sadducees say: "There is no resurrection of the dead, neither angel nor spirit," but the Pharisees acknowledge all of these.
And there was a great outcry. Some of the scribes from the Pharisees' party in the council stood up and argued, saying: "We find nothing evil in this man. A spirit has spoken to him, or an angel."
And as the dissension grew great, the tribune was afraid that Paul would be torn apart by them. He ordered the troops to go down, snatch him out from among them, and bring him into the barracks.
The following night the Lord stood by him and said to him: "Do not be afraid, for just as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify in Rome as well."
When it was day, the Jews formed an assembly and bound themselves under a curse, and said they would neither eat nor drink until they had killed Paul.
There were more than forty who made this conspiracy.
They went to the chief priests and the elders and said: "We have bound ourselves under a solemn curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.

Now therefore you, together with the council, inform the tribune so that he brings him down to you, as though you wished to examine his case more accurately; and we are ready to kill him before he comes near."
Paul's nephew heard of this plot. He went and entered the barracks and told Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions and said to him: "Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him."
So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said: "The prisoner Paul called me and asked me to bring this young man to you."
The tribune took him by the hand, led him aside privately, and asked him: "What is it that you have to tell me?"
He said: "The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to their council tomorrow, as though they intended to judge his case more accurately.

But do not give in to them, for more than forty of their men are lying in wait for him, who have bound themselves under a curse neither to eat nor drink until they have killed him; and now they are ready and waiting for your order."
So the tribune dismissed the young man and ordered him to tell no one: "You have informed me of this."
Then he called two of the centurions and said: "Get ready two hundred soldiers to go as far as Caesarea, along with seventy horsemen and two hundred shield-bearers, from the third hour of the night.
And prepare [?], so that they may set Paul on them and bring him to Felix the governor."
And he wrote a letter of the following form:
"[?] Lysias, to the most excellent Felix the governor, greetings.
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the troops and rescued him, having learned that he is a Roman.
Wishing to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council,
And I found that they were accusing him over questions of their law, and no charge deserving death or chains was found against him.
And when I was told of the evil plot against this man, I sent him to you, and I have ordered his accusers to state their case before you. Farewell!"
So the soldiers, as they had been ordered, took Paul and brought him by night as far as Antipatris.
And the next day they sent the horsemen on with him and returned to the camp.
And these entered Caesarea, gave the letter to the governor, and presented Paul to him as well.
He read it and asked, "Which province are you from?" And he learned that he was a Cilician.
He said, "I will hear you when your accusers also arrive." And he ordered him to be kept in Herod's palace.
After five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and with an orator named Tertullus, and they brought their case before the governor.
And when he had been called, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: "We enjoy great peace through you, and the reforms being made in this nation through your foresight
we welcome everywhere and in every place, most excellent Felix, with all gratitude.
I beg you, so as not to weary you any further, to hear us briefly in your kindness.
For we have found this man to be vile, one who stirs up unrest among all the Jews throughout the whole world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Galileans,
who even tried to defile the temple. We seized him,
and by examining him yourself you will be able to learn about all these things of which we accuse him."
The other Jews also testified against him, saying that this was so.
When the governor nodded to him, Paul answered and said: "Knowing that you have been judge of this nation for many years, I gladly make my defense.
You can confirm that it is no more than twelve days since I went up to Jerusalem to worship.
They did not find me in the temple speaking with anyone or stirring up a crowd, nor in the synagogues, nor in the city.
Nor can they prove to you the things of which they now accuse me.
But this I confess to you: that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I serve the God of our fathers, and I believe everything that is written in the prophets.
And I have a hope in God, which they themselves also look for, that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and sinners.
For this reason I also strive always to keep a clear conscience before God and before people.
And after many years I came to bring alms to my nation, and offerings.
While I was doing this they found me in the temple, purified, with no crowd and no disturbance.
But there were some Jews from Asia, and they are the ones who should have come before you to accuse me, if they have anything to say against me.
Or let these men themselves say what fault they found in me when I stood before the council,
unless it is about that one statement I cried out while I stood among them: 'It is about the resurrection of the dead that I am being judged by you.'"
Felix put them off, since he had accurate knowledge of the Way, and said: "When Lysias the tribune comes, then I will look into your case."
And he ordered the centurion to keep him in custody, but to let him be at ease, and not to stop any of his own people from serving him.
Some days later Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was a Jew. He summoned Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus.
And as Paul spoke to him about righteousness, self-restraint and the judgement to come, Felix became afraid and said: "That is enough for now. Go, and when I have a free moment I will summon you."
At the same time he was hoping that Paul would give him money. For this reason he kept summoning him again and again and talking with him.
When two years had passed, Porcius Festus came to Felix as [successor? literally 'servant']. Felix wanted to do the Jews a favour, so he left Paul in chains.
When Festus had arrived in the province, after three days he went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
The chief priests and the leaders of the Jews brought information to him against Paul.
They pleaded with him and asked him for a favour against Paul: to summon him to Jerusalem. They planned to lie in wait on the road to kill him.
But Festus told them that Paul was being kept in custody at Caesarea, and that he himself would soon be leaving Jerusalem.
And he said: "Let those of you who are able come with me, and if there is anything wrong with the man, bring your accusation against him."
He stayed there no more than eight or ten days, and then went down to Caesarea. He sat on the judgement seat and ordered Paul to be brought in.
When Paul came, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him and brought many serious charges against him, which they could not prove.
But Paul answered in his defence: "I have done no wrong at all, either against the law of the Jews or against Caesar."
But Festus wanted to do the Jews a favour, so he answered Paul and said: "Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be tried there before me on these charges?"
Paul said to him: "I am standing at Caesar's judgement seat, where I ought to be tried. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you know very well.

If I have done wrong and have committed something that deserves death, I do not try to escape death. But if I have done none of the things these men accuse me of, no one has the power to hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar."
Then Festus talked it over with his council and said: "You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you shall go."
Some days later King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus.
Since they were staying there many days, Festus told the king about Paul, saying: "There is a man here whom Felix left behind as a prisoner.
When I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews brought information to me about him and asked for a sentence against him.
I answered them that it is not the custom of the Romans to hand over any man before the accused has met his accusers face to face and has had a chance to make his defence against the charge.
So when they had gathered here, I did not delay at all. The next day I sat on the judgement seat and ordered the man to be brought in,
When the accusers stood up against him, they brought no charge of the evil that I had supposed;
they had certain disputes with him about their own superstition [lit. "their own demon"] and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul says is alive.
And since I found nothing by which to investigate this, I asked him whether he would be willing to go to Jerusalem and be judged there about these matters.
But Paul cried out to be kept in custody, so that Caesar might take cognizance of his case. So I ordered him to be kept until I send him to Caesar."
Agrippa answered and said to Festus, "I too would like to hear the man." And he said to him, "Tomorrow you shall hear him."

On the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp. And when they had entered the hall of judgment together with the commanders of thousands and the leading men of the city, Festus gave the order, and Paul came.

And Festus said, "King Agrippa, and all you men who are here with us, do you see this man? Concerning him the whole multitude of the Jews approached me in Jerusalem, and here too they are crying out and saying that he ought not to live any longer.
But I understood that he had done nothing deserving death; and since he appealed to Caesar, I decided to send him.

Yet I have nothing certain to write to my lord about him. That is why I have brought him before you, and above all before you, King Agrippa, so that you may examine him and I may know what to write about him.
For it seems unreasonable to me to send a prisoner and not make known the charge against him."
Then Agrippa said to Paul, "You are permitted to speak for yourself." Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defence, saying:
"Regarding all the things of which the Jews accuse me, King Agrippa, I count myself blessed that I am to make my defence before you today above all,
for you are well acquainted with all the customs and questions of the Jews and know them. Therefore I beg you to hear me patiently.
My way of life from my youth, which from the beginning was spent among my own nation in Jerusalem, is known to all the Jews.
They have known me from the beginning, if they are willing to testify, that I lived as a Pharisee in accordance with the truth of our religious service.
And now I stand and am judged for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers,
which our twelve tribes, earnestly serving day and night, hope to attain; and it is for this hope, O king, that I am accused.
Why is it judged unbelievable among you that God raises the dead?
I myself thought I ought to do many evil things against the name of Jesus the Nazarene,

and that is what I did in Jerusalem. I shut up many of the saints in prison, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were to be put to death I cast my vote [lit. "I took a count"] against them.
And in all the synagogues I punished them many times and forced them to blaspheme; and being furiously enraged against them, I persecuted them even as far as the surrounding cities.
While doing this I was travelling to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests.
At midday on the road, O king, I saw a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, shining around me and those travelling with me.
And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, 'Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad.'
I said, "Who are you, Lord?" And the Lord said to me, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
But rise and stand on your feet, for I have appeared to you for this reason: to appoint you as a servant and a witness of what you have seen of me and of what I will show you,
delivering you from the people and from the nations to whom I am sending you,

to open their eyes and to turn them from darkness to light and from the power of the devil to God, so that they may receive forgiveness of their sins and a share among those who are sanctified by faith in me."
Therefore, King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to that heavenly vision,

but I proclaimed first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the land of Judea, and to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to the living God, and do deeds worthy of repentance.
For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and plotted to kill me.
With help from God I stand to this very day, testifying to small and great alike, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass:
that the Christ was to suffer, and that he, first through the resurrection of the dead, would proclaim light to the people and to the nations."
As he was saying this, Festus said in a loud voice, "You are raving, Paul! Your many books are driving you to madness."
But Paul said, "I am not raving, noble Festus; I am speaking words of truth and soundness.
For the king, to whom I speak boldly, knows about these things. I do not believe that any of this is hidden from him, for this was not done in a hidden place.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe."
And Agrippa said to Paul, "A little more, and you will persuade me to become a Christian."
And Paul said to him, "I pray to God that, whether in little or in much, not only you but all who hear me today may become such as I am, except for these chains."
Then the king rose, and the governors, and Bernice, and those who were sitting with them.
And when they had gone out, they spoke with one another and said, "This man is doing nothing that deserves death or chains."
And Agrippa said to Festus, "This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar."
And when it was decided that we should sail by ship to Rome, they handed Paul and some other prisoners over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan cohort.
We boarded a ship from Adramyttium that was bound for the ports of Asia, and we set out. Aristarchus the Macedonian was with us.
The next day we reached Sidon. Julius treated Paul kindly and allowed him to go to his friends to be cared for.
From there we embarked again and sailed along under the shelter of Cyprus, because the wind was against us.
Then we crossed the open sea off Cilicia and came to Myra, a city of Lycia.
There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship that was sailing to Italy, and he put us on board it.
We sailed slowly for many days and with difficulty reached Cnidus, because the wind would not let us go further. Then we sailed along the coast of Crete, off Salmone.
And when we had passed it with difficulty, we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.
And when much time had passed and sailing was now dangerous, because the Fast was already over, Paul spoke
and said to them: "Men, I see that there is going to be hardship and loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but our own lives are also going to be lost along with the ship."
But the centurion trusted the pilot and the owner of the ship more than Paul's words.

And because the harbour was unsuitable for wintering, the majority [?] decided to set sail from there, in case they could somehow reach Phoenix and spend the winter there, at that harbour of Crete which faces north and toward the land.
And a south wind was blowing, and they supposed that things would go as they wished. They set out from Assos and were sailing along by Crete.
Not much time had passed when a whirlwind began against it, the one called "Broad Wave."
And when it struck the ship and the ship could not turn its face to the wind, we gave way and were driven this way and that.
We came under the lee of a certain island called Cauda, and with difficulty we managed to secure the ship's boat.
They hoisted it up, used supports, and bound them around the ship. And because they were afraid of running aground on a shoal, they let down the ship's gear, and so it was driven along.
And since we were in a great storm, from the next day on they began throwing the cargo overboard.
And on the third day they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands.
Neither stars nor sun appeared for many days, because the storm was great. From then on we gave up all hope of being saved.

And they had gone a long time without food. Then Paul stood up among them and said: "Men, you should have listened to me and not set out from Crete, and so brought this hardship and loss on yourselves.
And now I tell you: take heart, for not one of you will lose his life; only the ship will be lost.
For this night an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I serve stood beside me
and said to me: 'Do not be afraid, Paul! You must stand before Caesar, and see, God has granted you all those who are with you in this ship.'
So take heart, men, for I trust God that it will be just as he told me.
We must run aground on a certain island."
When the fourteenth night came and we were being driven this way and that in the Adriatic, around midnight the sailors began to suspect that they were nearing some land.
And they let down the sounding line and found twenty fathoms; after waiting a little they measured again and found twelve fathoms.
And because they were afraid of running aground on a rocky place, they let down four anchors from the stern of the ship and prayed for daylight to come.
But the sailors intended to escape from the ship, and they let the boat down into the sea, pretending that they were going to lay out the anchors.
Then Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers: "Unless these men stay in this ship, you cannot be saved."
Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the boat and let it go, and the waves carried it away.
When day dawned, Paul urged everyone to take food. He said: "Today is the fourteenth day since we set out. You have gone on fasting and have taken nothing.
So I urge you to take food, because this is for your survival. Not one hair of the head of any of you will perish."
When he had said this, he took bread and gave thanks to God in front of them all. Then he broke it and began to eat.
They all took heart, and they too asked for food.
In all, there were two hundred and seventy-six of us on the ship.
When they had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat overboard into the sea.
When day dawned, they did not recognize the land. But they noticed a bay with a shore, and they meant to drive the ship onto it if they somehow could.
They cut away the anchors and left them in the sea. At the same time they loosened the lashings of the rudders. Then they raised the small sail and held on toward the shore with the wind.
They struck a place where two seas met and ran the ship aground. The bow stuck fast and could not be moved, but the stern was being broken up by the violence of the waves.
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim away and escape.
But the centurion wanted to save Paul, and he stopped them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to get out by swimming,
and the rest to get out, some on planks and some on pieces of the ship. In this way we all came out and reached land safely.
Once we had come out, they learned that the island was called Malta.
The heathen people there showed us no small kindness. Because of the rain that had set in and the cold, they lit a fire and welcomed us all.
Paul was gathering a large bundle of brushwood and putting it on the fire when a viper came out because of the heat and fastened onto his hand.
When the heathen people saw the snake hanging from his hand, they said to one another: "This man must surely be a murderer. Even though he escaped from the sea, Justice has not allowed him to live."
But he shook the snake off into the fire and suffered no harm.

They expected him to swell up and suddenly fall down dead. But after they had stood watching for a long time and saw that nothing bad happened to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.
Near that place were estates belonging to the chief man of the island, whose name was Publius. He welcomed us and gave us generous, loving hospitality.
Publius's father was lying ill with fever and dysentery. Paul went in to see him, prayed, laid his hands on him and healed him.
After this happened, the other people on the island who had illnesses also came and were healed.
They honoured us with many honours, and when we left they loaded us with provisions for the journey.
After three days we boarded a ship from Alexandria that had spent the winter at the island. It was named the Dioscuri.
We sailed down to Syracuse and stayed there for three days.
From there we sailed around and reached Rhegium. After one day a south wind came up, and on the second day we arrived at Puteoli,
where we found brothers, and they begged us to stay with them seven days. And so we came to Rome.
From there the brothers heard about us and came to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns. When Paul saw them, he thanked God and took courage.
And when he entered Rome, Paul was allowed to stay by himself with the soldier who guarded him.

And after three days Paul called together those who were the leaders of the Jews. And when they had gathered, he said to them: "Men, brothers, I have done nothing wrong against the people or the law of our fathers, yet I was handed over as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans,
who examined me and wanted to release me, because there was no charge against me deserving death;
but when the Jews spoke against me, I was compelled to appeal to Caesar, not that I had any accusation to bring against my own nation.
For this reason I have asked you to come, so that I might see you and speak with you, for it is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain."
But they said to him: "We have received no letter about you from Judea, and none of the brothers has come and reported to us or said anything evil about you.
But we ask to hear from you what you think. For concerning this sect, we know that everywhere it is spoken against."

And they set a day, and many came to him at his lodging. From morning until evening he taught them and testified to the kingdom of God, and tried to convince them about Jesus from the law of Moses and from the prophets.
And some were persuaded by his words, and some did not believe.
They disagreed among themselves and began to leave. Paul said one thing: "The Holy Spirit spoke rightly to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet
when he said: 'Go to this people and say to them: You will keep hearing but will not understand, and you will keep seeing but will not perceive.'

For the heart of this people has grown dull, and they have become hard of hearing, and they have shut their eyes, so that they may not see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn back, and I would heal them.'
So let it be known to you that this salvation has been sent to the Gentiles; they will listen."
And he stayed there two whole years at his own expense, and welcomed all who came to him,
preaching the kingdom of God and teaching about Jesus Christ with complete boldness and without hindrance.
